newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders seek double success on EMU and treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders seek double success on EMU and treaty.

text.p: European Union leaders looked set on Monday to mend fences between France and Germany, the bloc's twin political and economic powerhouses, at a two-day summit which has been overshadowed by a row over monetary union.
The heads of government began the painstaking business of putting finishing touches to a new EU treaty, designed to pave the way for the 15-member bloc's enlargement and signal a Citizens' Europe.

Their finance ministers were to reconvene later in the morning (0900 GMT) to continue negotiations on the so-called stability pact, an accord reached in principle last December to stop countries running large deficits after the single currency is launched.
Diplomats said the leaders would try hard not to let a row between France and Germany over how to proceed with monetary union disrupt their negotiations of a new EU treaty.
"They are trying to do it in parallel, but (the row) also affects the mood," one said.

Arriving for the summit, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok admitted that the summit was effectively two-pronged -- agreeing the stability pact and finalising the inter-governmental conference (IGC) treaty review.
"We go for a double result. We want to have a good result on the treaty and, on top of that, we hope to have an agreement on the stability pact," he told reporters.

Over an informal dinner on Sunday, finance ministers appeared to get closer to a deal which could meet some French demands over employment without unravelling EMU's carefully laid plans and denting financial markets' confidence in the planned single currency.

The late-night meeting was forced on ministers when France's Socialist government refused to sign up to the stability pact, insisting that the EU should give job creation schemes as much priority as strict budgetary discipline.
Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinifto said early on Monday that a deal would be struck later today on conditions for EMU including the disputed budget stability pact.
"Big steps were taken yesterday. It's quite obvious there will be a good agreement about that (today)," he told Reuters.
However, the damaging rift between Paris and Bonn has laid bare the two core EU members' fundamental differences over how to cement monetary union, due to be launched in January 1999.
"In Germany there is a real distrust of everything political," Luxembourg Premier Jean-Claude Juncker said in an interview in Le Figaro. "In France there is a real distrust of everything economic."

Few details of the stability pact were available late on Sunday, but it appeared that France's pertners were unwilling to go as far as to promise support for large funding projects to chip away at the bloc's double-digit unemployment.

Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said the ministers had also discussed the possibility of giving the European Investment Bank (EIB), the bloc's main lending arm, a more active role in job creation.

EU leaders will be asked later by their finance colleagues to decide whether or not to hold a special "jobs summit" in Luxembourg in October, where they could focus more directly on France's desire to put employment at the top of the agenda.
